props.title: What we changed, what's blocked, and what each next step actually means
props.subtitle: The 3-hour optimization goal is done. This page decodes the parts that came out of it in shorthand.
props.meta: July 4, 2026 · session receipts committed at e75b51266

props.content: Overnight, the grammar parser got 2.3× faster and closed a third of its accuracy gap against the regex parser — without moving a single scored baseline row. Along the way it hit walls that are not grammar-code problems: missing vocabulary catalogs, an unreviewed data file, a test that needs servers running. Those walls are the 'wider-change notes.' This page explains each one, what performance work is still on the table, and what every item on the next-steps list would actually do.

props.content:
Quick refresher so the rest of the page makes sense. The system has **two parsers** for controller speech: the **regex lane** (production, 97% correct, powers today's baseline) and the **grammar lane** (the Earley chart parser — structured, explainable, better at garbled audio, but younger). The long game is for grammar to earn its way into production row by row.

Two measurements matter. The **baseline** (`just baseline`) is the referee: 1,262 scored turns across four corpora. It ran three times tonight with a row-by-row diff — nothing moved, which is the proof that all the speed and coverage work changed *how* answers are computed, never *what* they are. The **head-to-head** is a side-by-side: give both parsers the same 1,163 utterances and compare against gold. Grammar went from 58.4% to 68.0% fully-correct tonight. The remaining 30% gap is what the next-steps list is about.

props.label: PART 1
props.title: The wider-change notes, explained
props.subtitle: The goal locked all edits to grammar code. These six things need changes elsewhere — data files, authority modules, infrastructure — so they were logged instead of done. Here is what each one means and what fixing it buys.

props.content: A core anti-cheat rule in this repo: **the grammar never invents vocabulary**. Every word it recognizes — airline names, airport names, facility names — must come from a governed catalog file in `data/atc/`, so that what the system understands is auditable data, not code. That rule is why most of these notes exist: the grammar code is now *ready* for more vocabulary, but the catalogs themselves are thin, and filling them is data-lane work with its own review process.

props.title: 🧱 1 · Reserved-word universe
props.content: THE PROBLEM: A pilot can say 'contact Huntsville approach' for any facility in the country. Tonight I tried letting the grammar accept ANY unknown word before 'approach/tower/ground' as a facility name. The test suite caught it immediately: the parser started swallowing neighbors — it read 'contact tower' as a facility literally named 'contact', and grabbed 'xray' out of a callsign tail to make 'xray tower'. THE FIX: before trusting an unknown word as a name, the grammar needs a computed list of words that are already claimed — command verbs like 'contact', phonetic letters like 'xray', numbers. That list must be derived from templates and catalogs (not hand-written, which would break anti-cheat), and lexeme code can't see templates today. Small design slice, big payoff: nationwide facility call-ups.

props.title: 📚 2 · Catalog gaps (the biggest lever)
props.content: THE PROBLEM: The facility catalog has 36 entries — demo airports only. And two vocabulary types, WIND and POSITION, have no accessor function at all in the authority module, so 7 phrase templates literally cannot compile. AIRPORT (8 templates) and REASON (8 templates) are in the same boat. In the head-to-head, a large share of the 349 utterances grammar still loses trace back to a word it has no catalog for. THE FIX: add the missing accessor functions to modules/authority/domain.py and expand the JSON catalogs in data/atc/vocab/. This is mostly data entry plus two small code hooks — and it is the single biggest accuracy lever available.

props.title: ⚠️ 3 · telephony.json is unreviewed
props.content: WHAT IT IS: the file mapping airline radio callsigns to spoken names ('Cactus' → US Airways style prefixes), used to recognize callsign starts. It is marked needs_review — nobody has verified its 36 entries against a real source. HOW WE STAYED SAFE: tonight's CALL_SIGN work uses it only to decide how far a callsign span extends; it never copies a value from it into any answer. THE ASK: someone reviews the file against FAA/ICAO telephony designators. Until then, do not let anything project values out of it.

props.title: 🔢 4 · Missing colloquial numbers
props.content: THE PROBLEM: the governed number catalog knows 'two zero' but not 'twenty'. A controller saying 'delay twenty minutes in holding' won't bind in the grammar lane, while the regex lane's free-text matcher shrugs and accepts it. This is documented in tests as an honest gap rather than papered over. THE FIX: add tens words ('twenty' through 'ninety') to data/atc/vocab/number_words.json — a data change with test coverage, an hour of work. It was out of scope only because it lives in data/, not grammar code.

props.title: 🔀 5 · Homophone list belongs in policy
props.content: WHAT IT IS: when audio garbles 'for' into 'four' or 'to' into 'two', the repair system treats them as sound-alikes at a discounted cost. That sound-alike list currently sits as a constant in scanner code. WHY MOVE IT: the repo's rule is that phrase knowledge lives in policy YAML (data/atc/policy/), where it can be reviewed and edited without a code deploy. grammar_repair_pricing.yaml already has an equivalent_sets concept — the list should move there. Pure hygiene, zero behavior change, keeps the anti-cheat boundary crisp.

props.title: 🎧 6 · Final-boss needs the stack up
props.content: WHAT IT IS: final-boss is the full end-to-end test — real audio in, speech recognition, intent parsing, readback out, speech synthesis — the closest thing to a live flight check. It needs ten local services running (ASR server, TTS server, intent daemon, etc.). They were all down at 3am, and starting a fleet of model servers unattended felt wrong, so it is the one gate honestly marked not-tested. THE FIX: two commands when you're at the machine: 'just dev local', then the recorded final-boss command from the handoff. ~15 minutes.

props.label: PART 2
props.title: Next performance ideas — and an honest ceiling
props.subtitle: Where the remaining milliseconds live, what could claw them back, and why accuracy is now the better investment.

props.content:
Before tonight, one stage — **column compaction** (deduplicating and pruning parser states) — ate 54% of every parse. That is gone: compaction is down to 20.6%, and the two fallback stages (island parsing and partial-match rebuilds) collapsed from half a minute of combined work per run to a couple of seconds. What remains is the **chart loop itself**: the fundamental scan-predict-advance cycle of the Earley algorithm, now 87.6% of a much smaller number.

That matters for what comes next: there is no single fat target left. The remaining ideas are each worth maybe 10–25%, not 2×, and the riskier ones trade exactness for speed. Meanwhile the current p50 of **158ms is already comfortably inside the voice budget** — a pilot pause between transmissions is 700ms+. Speed is no longer the bottleneck; the 30% accuracy gap is.

props.title: The honest read
props.content: Only the first idea is worth doing casually — it is safe and provable with the golden-replay harness that already exists. Everything below it should wait until there is a latency requirement that 158ms fails to meet. Right now no such requirement exists, and every hour on the accuracy gap moves a number that operators actually feel.

props.label: PART 3
props.title: The next-steps list, decoded
props.subtitle: Each option from the goal-complete report: what it literally is, why it is on the list, and what you get out of it.

props.title: 1 · Rerun final-boss  —  the 15-minute confidence check
props.content: WHAT: bring the local service stack up ('just dev local') and run the full audio-to-readback pipeline test once. WHY: it is the only verification gate from tonight marked not-tested, purely because the servers were off. WHAT YOU GET: either a clean green across the real pipeline — closing the last open loop on tonight's work — or an early warning that something integrates badly, caught before anyone flies with it. EFFORT: ~15 minutes, needs you at the machine.

props.title: 2 · Catalog-expansion slice  —  the biggest accuracy lever
props.content: WHAT: a scoped work package that (a) adds the two missing accessor functions (WIND, POSITION) to the authority module, and (b) grows the vocabulary catalogs — facilities beyond the 36 demo entries, AIRPORT names, REASON phrases. WHY: this is wider-change note #2. Dozens of the utterances grammar still loses in the head-to-head fail on a missing word, not missing logic — the parser is ready, the dictionary is thin. WHAT YOU GET: template universe grows from 443 toward ~470, and the head-to-head number moves several points without touching parser code. This is data work with review gates, so it goes through /propose as its own slice rather than being snuck in.

props.title: 3 · Reserved-word universe slice  —  unlock unknown facility names
props.content: WHAT: the designed fix for wider-change note #1. Build a computed set of 'claimed' words (template verbs, phonetic alphabet, number words — derived from existing catalogs and templates, never hand-listed), expose it to the vocabulary resolvers, then re-enable the rule that an unknown word before 'approach/tower/center' is a facility name. WHY: tonight's attempt proved the guardrail is the missing piece — with it, 'contact Huntsville approach' parses anywhere in the country; without it, the parser eats its neighbors. WHAT YOU GET: facility call-ups stop depending on the catalog at all, which matters exactly in the situations BATC throws unscripted speech at the system. EFFORT: a real design slice — the claimed-word set must be derived, cached, and tested against the two failure cases tonight exposed.

props.title: 5 · Promote grammar-recoverable rows  —  grammar earns production trust
props.content: WHAT: 'promotion' means adding specific phrase templates to the short list the LIVE engine trusts the grammar to handle (today that list is ~52 of the 443 rows it can parse; everything else runs in shadow — parsed and logged, but the regex answer ships). Tonight's shadow data shows a set of B1 rows where grammar now consistently matches or beats regex. WHY: this is the actual long game — grammar replacing regex one proven row at a time. THE SAFETY RAIL: the '95.7% ratchet floor' is the standing rule that the scored baseline may never drop below its current 95.7% pass rate; every promotion runs the full baseline and reverts if the number so much as twitches. WHAT YOU GET: real production traffic moving to the structured parser, reversibly.

props.title: 6 · Say-again lane goal  —  spend the speed dividend on judgment
props.content: WHAT: a fresh timeboxed goal on the repair/clarification lane — the logic that decides when the system should ask the controller to 'say again' instead of acting on a shaky parse. WHY IT CONNECTS: earlier analysis found parser confidence is hardcoded to 1.0 on any match, so the system literally cannot tell a solid parse from a lucky one — 15 wrong-intent and 16 wrong-slot failures sail through invisible. Now that a full grammar parse costs 158ms instead of 461ms, we can afford to run BOTH parsers on every turn and use their DISAGREEMENT as the missing confidence signal: when regex and grammar read the same audio differently, that turn is exactly the one worth a clarifying question. WHAT YOU GET: fewer confidently-wrong readbacks — the most dangerous failure class in the system — traded for a handful of extra 'say again' turns.

props.title: 7 · Broad-golden CI canary  —  keep tonight's guarantees forever
props.content: WHAT: tonight's strongest safety tool was a harness that replays 388 real corpus utterances through the parser and diffs every detail of the outcome — it caught every equivalence question in minutes and currently lives in a session scratchpad, which evaporates. WHY: promote it into the repo as a nightly CI job (or pre-merge check on grammar files) so any future edit that silently changes parser behavior gets flagged the same night, not weeks later when a baseline row moves. WHAT YOU GET: tonight's '0 diffs across 7 replays' standard becomes a permanent, automatic property of the codebase. EFFORT: small — the harness exists; it needs a home under tooling/, a checked-in fixture, and a CI hook.

props.title: 4 & 8 · 'All of the above' and 'Back'  —  the meta-options
props.content: Option 4 chains the quick wins in order: final-boss check first (15 min), then the catalog slice and reserved-word slice queued through /propose as reviewable work packages. Option 8 simply returns to the standing pe-ratchet-99 loop — the normal background cadence of measure, fix one thing, re-measure — with tonight's faster parser and bigger universe as the new normal. Neither loses anything: every receipt, note, and disposition is committed in the handoff and the goal ledger.

props.title: Sequence: 1 → 7 → 2 → 5, and let 3 ride behind 2
props.content: Run final-boss while you have coffee (closes the only open gate). Land the CI canary the same day — it is cheap and it locks in every guarantee the rest of the plan depends on. Then the catalog slice, because it is the largest accuracy move with the smallest design risk. Promotion (5) follows naturally once the catalog work makes more rows provably safe, and the reserved-word slice (3) is the right second design task once the catalog shows which names still miss. The say-again goal (6) is the most interesting piece of engineering on this list — but it deserves its own 3-hour window, not the tail end of this one.
